activities.anchor: its timing is the war's signature
activities.caption: line up the independence dates, earliest first
activities.name: decolWavesOrder

config.prompt: The waves of decolonisation — order these by date, earliest first:
items: The United States, from thirteen British colonies — 1776
Seventeen African states at once — the Year of Africa — 1960
config.why: The first wave emptied the Americas; the great wave followed the Second World War — metropoles financially exhausted, armies beaten at Singapore in 1942, colonial soldiers denied the freedoms they had fought for, and both superpowers preaching self-determination. The UN grew from 51 members in 1945 to more than 140 by the mid-1970s.

activities.anchor: Historians describe a negotiation forced by
activities.caption: bet before you read on — the timetable's driver
activities.name: decolVoluntaryPredict

config.q: Why did the European empires actually dissolve on the timetable they did?
choices: Under pressure: mass movements, liberation wars, war debt and superpower disapproval
On a UN-administered schedule of referendums
config.why: Pressure drove it: the Indian National Congress's mass movements, the 1945–49 Indonesian and Indochinese wars, the Mau Mau emergency (1952–60), the Algerian war each raised the price of holding on — and grants of flags at ceremonies were the last act of a much longer drama.

activities.anchor: The sequel is instructive and often misread
activities.caption: pair each inherited artefact with its story
activities.name: decolInheritedMatch

config.prompt: The inherited state — pair each artefact with its history:

pairs.right: drawn in five weeks by a lawyer who had never been to India
boundaries drawn by imperial convenience — rivers, minerals, railway gauges
border inviolability, chosen to prevent a continent-wide war of revisions
wars within the inherited states, not between them

config.why: Around fifteen million people crossed the new borders of partitioned India in both directions; the borders were not drawn randomly — they were drawn deliberately for someone else's purposes.

activities.anchor: The fuel came from what the inherited states contained
activities.caption: true or false — the border indictment
activities.name: decolBordersJudge

statements.s: The colonial borders were drawn randomly.
statements.why: They were drawn deliberately — by imperial convenience; that is a different and more useful indictment.

statements.s: Newly independent African states chose to keep the colonial borders.
statements.why: The OAU's 1964 pledge of inviolability was itself a deliberate peace-keeping choice.

statements.s: Most post-colonial African conflicts have been interstate wars over where the lines lay.
statements.why: Most were civil wars over who controlled the inherited states — the borders set the stage; they did not write the play.

activities.caption: call the number — the pegged currency club
activities.name: decolCfaEstimate

config.prompt: How many African states kept the CFA franc, pegged to the franc and partly deposited with the French treasury?
config.why: Fourteen — monetary sovereignty visibly outsourced, Nkrumah's 'neocolonialism' made concrete.
config.context: In the mid-1970s copper supplied the great majority of Zambia's export earnings, so the 1975 slump turned a proud new state into an indebted one within a decade — no corruption required.

activities.anchor: The Cold War offered the new states a menu with two items, and they declined it
activities.caption: drag the divider — the two-item menu versus the third path
activities.name: decolThirdPathCompare

config.prompt: Bandung's answer to the blocs — drag the divider:

before.label: join a bloc
before.text: Patronage, arms and bases — at the price of becoming a client in someone else's war.

after.label: non-alignment
after.text: Bandung 1955 — twenty-nine Asian and African states, no colonisers in the room; Belgrade 1961 — a movement grown to some 120 members, converting the bidding war into leverage: Nasser took Soviet arms when the West refused the Aswan Dam; India took aid from both blocs.

config.why: An honest ledger: partial successes (the Suez humiliation of 1956 showed the old powers could no longer act alone) and failures (détente negotiated over the Global South's head).

activities.anchor: the colonised analysing the coloniser's account of them
activities.caption: line up the writing-back shelf, by year
activities.name: decolTurnOrder

config.prompt: The postcolonial turn — order these by publication year, earliest first:
items: Fanon, The Wretched of the Earth — 1961
Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o, Decolonising the Mind — 1986
config.why: From psychology (liberation is psychological as much as legal), to the image of 'the East' built as an instrument of rule, to the language question, to the methodological problem of recovering the subaltern's voice — an argument that now continues in institutions: Rhodes Must Fall, renamed universities, the returning Benin Bronzes.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the divergence seminar
activities.name: decolDivergenceSpot

config.prompt: One line of this divergence seminar is wrong — click it:
lines: Singapore and South Korea were both poor and post-colonial in 1960.
Both reached high income within two generations.
Commodity-rich states with comparable starting points did the same.
Initial conditions, policy choices and contingency all appear in the winning cases.
The 'one secret of development' genre sells well and proves little.
config.correction: Commodity-rich states with comparable starting points did not converge — which is exactly why the honest literature refuses a single cause.
config.why: Settler institutions versus extraction colonies, human capital at independence, export discipline versus import substitution, tenure and luck all appear in the winning cases — no one secret.
